¶
'''wieldable''' (wēl′da-bl), ''a.'' [< ''wield'' + ''-able''.] Capable of being wielded.

'''wieldance†''' (wēl′dans), ''n.'' [< ''wield'' + ''-ance''.] The act or power of wielding. ''Bp. Hall'', St. Paul’s Combat, ii.

'''wielder''' (wēl′dėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''weldere'', possessor (= G. ''walter'' = Icel. ''valdari'', ''valdr'', ruler); < ''wield'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who wields, employs, manages, or possesses.
{{smaller block|Like the fabled spear of old mythology, endued with the faculty of healing the saddest wound its most violent ''wielder'' can inflict.
{{right|''Landor'', Imag. Conv., Melanchthon and Calvin.}}
<poem>Brisk ''wielder'' of the birch and rule,
The master of the village school.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', Snow-Bound.}}}}

'''wieldiness''' (wēl′di-nes), ''n.'' The property of being wieldy.

'''wielding†''' (wēl′ding), ''n.'' [< ME. ''weeldynge''; verbal n. of ''wield'', ''v.''] Management; control.
{{smaller block|Ye have hem in youre myght and in youre ''weeldynge''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Tale of Melibeus.}}}}

'''wieldless''' (wēld′les), ''a.'' [Early mod. E. ''weeldlesse''; < ''wield'' + ''-less''.] Unmanageable; unwieldy.
{{smaller block|<poem>That with the weight of his owne ''weeldlesse'' might
He falleth nigh to ground, and scarse recovereth flight.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. iii. 19.}}}}

'''wieldsome†''' (wēld′sum), ''a.'' [< ''wield'' + ''-some''. Cf. (for the form) G. ''gewaltsam'', violent, pow-

''geweldan'', ''gewyldan'', have power over; a secondary form of the strong verb, ME. ''walden'', ''wealden'' (pret. ''wield''), < AS. ''wealdan'' (pret. ''weóld'', pp. ''wealden''), have power over, govern, rule, possess, = OS. ''waldan'' = OFries. ''walda'' = D. ''welden'' = OHG. ''waltan'', dispose, manage, rule, MHG. G. ''walten'', rule, = Icel. ''valda'', wield, = Sw. ''välla'' (for *''välda''), occasion, cause, = Dan. ''volde'', commonly ''for-volde'', occasion, cause, = Goth. ''waldan'', govern; cf. Russ. ''vladieti'', reign, rule, possess, make use of, = Lith. ''waldyti'', rule, govern, possess; prob. < L. ''valere'', be strong, have power: see ''valid''.]   '''1.''' To have power or sway over; rule; govern; manage. {{smaller block|Now coronyd is the kyng this cuntre to ''weld''; Hade homage of all men, & honour full grete, And began for to gouerne, as gome in his owne. {{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 5381.}}}} {{smaller block|Adam . . . ''welte'' al Paradys, saving o tree. {{right|''Chaucer'', Monk’s Tale, l. 20.}}}} {{smaller block|Thence to the famous orators repair, Those ancient, whose resistless eloquence ''Wielded'' at will that fierce democratie, Shook the arsenal, and fulmined over Greece. {{right|''Milton'', P. R., iv. 269.}}}} {{smaller block|Where’er that Power may move . . . Which ''wields'' the world with never-wearied love. {{right|''Shelley'', Adonais, xlii.}}}} '''2.''' To use or exert in governing; sway. {{smaller block|Her new-born power was ''wielded'' at the first by unprincipled and ambitious men.{{right|''De Quincey.''}}}} '''3.''' Hence, in general, to exercise; put to practical or active use, as a means, an instrument, or a weapon; use with freedom and ease: as, to ''wield'' a hammer. {{smaller block|Ac his witt ''welt'' he after as wel as to-fore.{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 142.}}}} {{smaller block|In oure chapitre praye we day and nyght To Crist that he thee sende heele and myght Thy body for to ''weelden'' hastily.{{right|''Chaucer'', Summoner’s Tale, l. 239.}}}} {{smaller block|Part ''wield'' their arms, part curb the foaming steed.{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 643.}}}} {{smaller block|A potent wand doth Sorrow ''wield''.{{right|''Wordsworth'', Peter Bell.}}}} '''4†.''' To have; possess; enjoy. {{smaller block|And sum prince axide him, seyinge, Good maister, what thing doynge schal I ''welde'' euerlastyng lyf?{{right|''Wyclif'', Luke xviii. 18.}}}} {{smaller block|And alway [he] slewe the kynges dere, And ''welt'' them at his wyll.{{right|''Lytell Geste of Robyn Hode'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 108).}}}} {{smaller block|But tell me, that hast seen him, Menaphon, What stature ''wields'' he, and what personage?{{right|''Marlowe'', Tamburlaine, I., ii. 1.}}}} '''To wield a good baton.''' {{smaller|See ''baton''.}} '''wield†''', ''n.''   [< ME. A woman who is united to a man in the lawful bonds of wedlock; a man’s spouse: the correlative of ''husband.'' He ȝede forth bliue To Rymenhild his ''wyue.'' {{smaller block|{{right|''King Horn'' (E. Taylor.''}}}} '''All the world and his wife.''' {{smaller|See ''world.''}}—'''Auld wives’ tongues.''' {{smaller|See ''auld.''}}—'''Deceased Wife’s Sister Bill.''' {{smaller|See ''bill''3.}}—'''Dutch wife.''' {{smaller|See ''Dutch.''}}—'''Inhibition against a wife.''' {{smaller|See ''inhibition.''}}—'''Old wife.''' {{smaller|See ''old.''}}—'''Old wives’ tale.''' {{smaller|See ''tale''1.}}—'''Plural wives,''' {{smaller|consorts or concubines of the same man under a polygamous union.}}—'''Ratification by a wife.''' {{smaller|See ''ratification.''}}—'''Wife’s equity,''' {{smaller|in ''law,'' the general rule established by courts of equity that where a husband resorted to a court of equity to enforce his common law marital right to take his wife’s property, that court would, in general, oblige him to make a reasonable provision out of the fund for the benefit of his wife and children. Of high Carthage? {{right|''Surrey'', Æneid, iv. 343.}}}} '''wife-carl''' (wīf′kärl), ''n.'' A man who busies himself about household affairs or woman’s work. [Scotch.] '''wifehood''' (wīf′hu̇d), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wifhod'', ''wiifhood'', < AS. ''wīfhād'', < ''wīf'', wife, + ''hād'', condition.]   Wifely character or condition; the state of being a wife. {{smaller block|She taughte al the craft of fyn lovinge, And namely of ''wyfhood'' the livinge.{{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 545.}}}} {{smaller block|The stately flower of female fortitude,

'''wifeless''' (wīf′les), ''a.''   [< ME. ''wiifles'', ''wyfles'', ''wyflees''; < ''wife'' + ''-less''.]   Without a wife; unmarried. {{smaller block|Sixty yeer a ''wyflees'' man was he.{{right|''Chaucer'', Merchant’s Tale, l. 4.}}}} '''wifelike''' (wīf′līk), ''a.''   [< ''wife'' + ''-like''.]   Resembling or pertaining to a wife or woman. {{smaller block|''Wifelike'' government. {{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., ii. 4. 138.}}}} {{smaller block|''Wifelike'', her hand in one of his.{{right|''Tennyson'', Aylmer’s Field.}}}} '''wifely''' (wīf′li), ''a.''   [< ME. ''wifly'', ''wifli'', < AS. ''wīflīc'', < ''wīf'', wife + ''-līc'', E. ''-ly''1.]   Pertaining to or befitting a wife; like a wife. {{smaller block|Yit is it bet for me For to be deed in ''wyfly'' honestee Than be a traitour living in my shame.{{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 2701.}}}} {{smaller block|With all the tenderness of ''wifely'' love. {{right|''Dryden'', Amphitryon, iii.}}}} '''wife-ridden''' (wīf′rid″n), ''a.'' Unduly influenced by a wife; ruled or tyrannized over by a wife; henpecked. {{smaller block|Listen not to those sages who advise you always to scorn the counsel of a woman, and if you comply with her requests pronounce you ''wife-ridden.'' {{right|''Mrs. Piozzi.''}}}} '''wiflet†''', ''n.''   [Origin obscure.]   A kind of ax. {{smaller block|xj. crosbowes whereof iij. of stele, and v wyndas. Item, j. borespere. Item, vj. ''wifles.'' {{right|''Paston Letters'', I. 487.}}}} '''wifman†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''woman.'' '''wig1†''', ''n.''   [< ME. ''wig'', < AS. ''wicg'' = Icel. ''viggr'' (''viggja-''), also ''vigg'', a horse, steed; connected with AS. ''wegan'', carry: see ''way''1, ''weigh''1.]   A beast of burden, as a horse or an ass. {{smaller block|Ac theh he [were] alre louerdes louerd, and alre kingene ki[n]g, natheles he sende after the alre unwurtheste ''wig'' one to riden, and that is asse. {{right|''Old Eng. Homilies'', 2d ser., p. 89.}}}} '''wig2''' (wig), ''n.''   [Also ''wigg'' (and erroneously ''whig''); early mod. E. ''wygge''; = D. ''wig'', ''wigge'', a wedge, = G. ''weck'', ''wecke'', a sort of bread: see ''wedge''1.]   A sort of cake. [Obsolete or local.] {{smaller block|Home to the only Lenten supper I have had of ''wiggs'' and ale. {{right|''Pepys'', Diary, II. 117.}}}} {{smaller block|You may make ''wigs'' of the biscuit dough, by adding . . . currans. {{right|''Coll. of Receipts'', p. 2. (''Jamieson.'')}}}} '''wig'''3 (wig), ''n.''   [Abbr. of ''periwig'': see ''periwig'' {{img float|file=century v08 p0726 c3f1.png|width=100px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Forms of Wig worn in Great Britain in the 17th and 18th centuries.}}
{{smaller|1, Time of James I.; 2, time of Charles I.; 3, 4, 5, Restoration, Charles II.; 6, 7, time of James II. and Anne; 8, 9, time of William and Mary; 10, campaign wig, 1684; 11, Ramilie wig, 1736; 12, bob-wig, 1742; 13, 14, the Macaronis’ wig, 1772; 15, 16, wigs of 1774-80; 17, 18, wigs of 1785-95.}}}} and ''peruke''.]   '''1.''' An artificial covering of hair for the head, used generally to conceal baldness, but formerly worn as a fashionable head-dress. {{smaller|Wigs are usually made to imitate the natural hair, but formal curled wigs are worn as part of their professional costume by judges and lawyers in Great Britain. Wigs are much used on the stage. See ''peruke''.}} {{smaller block|I have often wanted him to throw off his great flaxen ''wig''; . . . with his usual Gothic vivacity, he said I only wanted . . . to convert it into a tête for my own wearing. {{right|''Goldsmith'', She Stoops to Conquer, ii.}}}} {{smaller block|I never believe anything that a lawyer says when he has a ''wig'' on his head and a fee in his hand. {{right|''Trollope'', Phineas Redux, lxi.}}}} '''2.''' The full-grown male fur-seal of Alaska, ''Callorhinus ursinus''. See cut ununder ''fur-seal''.—'''3.''' The head. [Colloq.]—'''Allonge wig.'''
